newsitem.title: USA: Free-trading U.S. ag sector backs China MFN.
newsitem.headline: Free-trading U.S. ag sector backs China MFN.

text.p: Renewal of Most Favored Nation (MFN) trade for China is in the best interest of the export-oriented U.S. agriculture system, farm groups and analysts said Monday.

They foresaw a tougher fight than in the past to win congressional approval, partly because of qualms about the pending transfer of Hong Kong to Chinese control, Beijing's testy relations with Taiwan and concern over human rights.
President Clinton announced on Monday he had decided to extend MFN trade status for another year.
"We'll be happy to get 12 months," said Barbara Spangler, international trade specialist with the American Farm Bureau, the largest U.S. farm group.
"We really think the House is going to be a stomping ground for 'let's bash China,'" by congressional critics, she said.
Just back from Beijing, Spangler said Chinese officials made it clear they would play hardball on tariff issues with the United States if MFN was denied.
"They made that very clear to us, that they could play this game too," she said in a telephone interview.
China is one of the leading ag import markets of the world.
The National Association of Wheat Growers said it supported MFN renewal too.

"Failure to renew China's MFN status would put an end to our commercial agricultural relations, bringing an enormous negative impact to U.S. wheat farmers and the U.S. economy," the wheat growers group said.
Private consultant Bill Lesher said the ag sector, a longtime advocate of freer trade, favored MFN.
"It'll be a much closer vote (than in the past), I think, and the president is going to have to get some Democratic votes," Lesher said.
John Schnittker, a private consultant, described renewal of MFN as "a very mainstream decision which, while debated, was never in doubt" because of the administration's pro-business leanings.

The MFN decision, he said, "is far more important as a poltical move and for other sectors of the economy than agriculture, but even so, it is important for farmers even though the China market is somewhat volatile and uncertain, especially for grains."
China bought huge amounts of U.S. wheat in recent years but only 288,100 tonnes in the nearly ended 1996/97 marketing year.
There were many reasons for lawmakers to be cautious in facing the vote on China, analysts said.

"It's a little bit riskier vote this time from a political perspective," said one analyst, who asked not to be identified. As an example, he pointed to the potential for recriminations if Congress approves MFN for China but the take-over of Hong Kong goes poorly.
